name: DMAA (1,3-dimethylamylamine)

lead: DMAA, or 1,3-dimethylamylamine (also methylhexanamine), is a stimulant developed by Eli Lilly as an inhaled nasal decongestant and later sold in supplements for fat loss and workout energy. It was often paired with caffeine, in a combination that resembled the ephedrine-caffeine stack.

People used it because stimulants raise alertness and perceived training drive, which in the looksmaxxing chain means harder sessions and more calorie burn toward a leaner physique. Regulators in several countries have since banned or restricted it, and sports bodies prohibit it.

paras: It was taken orally as part of pre-workout and fat-burner blends, usually with caffeine, before training. Because it is now banned or restricted in many places, products containing it have mostly left mainstream supply.

The FDA says it narrows blood vessels and can raise blood pressure, and it has not accepted it as a legal supplement ingredient. At least five deaths have been linked to DMAA-containing supplements, and it is prohibited by WADA and many sports bodies.

angle.text: Users took it before workouts for energy and focus, and in fat-loss blends for the stimulant-driven effects on appetite and expenditure that users associated with ephedrine-type products.

lead: DMAA (1,3-dimethylamylamine, also called methylhexanamine, geranamine or 'geranium extract' on labels) is an indirect sympathomimetic stimulant. Eli Lilly marketed it as an inhaled nasal decongestant, Forthane, from the mid-1940s until withdrawing it in 1983. Chemist Patrick Arnold reintroduced it in 2006 as a supplement ingredient under the name Geranamine, shortly after the US final ephedrine ban in 2005 [1].

Supplement makers sold it in pre-workout and fat-loss products, usually alongside caffeine, a pairing the literature compares to the ephedrine-caffeine stack. Users took it for alertness, focus and a sense of training drive; in the looksmaxxing chain that means harder, longer sessions and more energy expenditure toward a leaner, more muscular physique [1][2][3]. Labels often said it came from geranium oil or extract, while Wikipedia reports that geranium oils are not found to contain it and that the added compound is synthetic [1]; a 2012 analytical paper examined that question [4].

Human studies include a 12-week randomized trial of caffeine and DMAA in 50 healthy men [5], a pharmacokinetic study in eight men [6] and a randomized trial of heart rate and blood pressure effects of DMAA with caffeine [7]. Regulators in many countries restricted it from 2010 onward, the US FDA considers products containing it illegal, and sports bodies prohibit it [1].
infobox: FDA: not a legal dietary ingredient; banned or restricted in many countries; WADA-prohibited [1]

paras: DMAA was used as a pre-workout stimulant and as a fat-loss ingredient, typically combined with caffeine [1]. Forum users described it as raising focus and drive in the gym; one T Nation member compared it favourably to caffeine, another called it a head rush that did not itself build muscle or strength, and others said it could interfere with evening sleep or called for breaks from use [2][8][9]. A looksmax.org thread asks whether a DMAA pre-workout is 'good', with replies repeating hearsay that it is 'insane' [10].
Its only medical use was as an inhaled nasal decongestant in the Forthane product; the FDA says it is no longer approved and that it recognises no medical use today [1].

DMAA constricts blood vessels and also produces bronchodilation, reduced intestinal motility and diuresis; much of the data comes from inhaled use, and oral effects are partly extrapolated from related compounds [1]. Rat studies published in 2019 and 2023 suggest it acts as a norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent [1]. A T Nation poster described it as structurally similar to amphetamine and working in the brain somewhat like it [11].

Wikipedia cites an elimination half-life of about 8.5 hours, so repeated use within 24 to 36 hours may accumulate [1]. A pharmacokinetic study in eight men measured both blood levels and physiological responses after oral administration, noting that no earlier study had done both [6].

The FDA says it knows of no information showing DMAA is safe, that it can raise blood pressure and has been linked to cardiovascular problems including heart attack, as well as seizures and neurological and psychological conditions, and that risk is greater alongside stimulants such as caffeine. At least five deaths have been associated with supplements containing it [1].

Reported cases include a 21-year-old in New Zealand who had a cerebral hemorrhage in 2010 after taking it with caffeine and alcohol, and Claire Squires, who collapsed near the finish of the April 2012 London Marathon; the coroner said DMAA was 'probably an important factor', as reported by the BBC in January 2013 [1]. A 2013 pharmacokinetic paper notes that doses above recommended amounts in party pills have been associated with cerebral hemorrhage [6]. Wikipedia also lists a 2023 case report linking it to secondary open-angle glaucoma [1].

A 2012 US Department of Defense safety panel, with its report dated June 2013, found that the evidence did not conclusively prove causation but recommended keeping the ban on sales at military exchanges [1].

Eli Lilly introduced Forthane in the 1940s; Wikipedia gives April 1944 in the text and 1948 in the infobox, and the new drug application was withdrawn in 1983 [1]. Arnold's company, Proviant Technologies, held the Geranamine name when it reappeared in 2006 [1]. Supplements often claimed a geranium origin [1][4].

The compound became widely visible through pre-workout products. In 2010 the US military removed DMAA products from exchange stores worldwide [1]. In 2013 the FDA administratively detained OxyElite Pro and Jack3d, two USPLabs products, and USPLabs later destroyed them and agreed to stop using DMAA; Hawaii health authorities had separately linked liver failure cases and one death to OxyElite Pro [1].

The FDA says DMAA is not a dietary ingredient, that supplements containing it are illegal, and that it knows of no reliable science showing it occurs naturally in plants. It lists warning letters from 24 April 2012 to ten companies including USP Labs, and further letters in 2012, 2013, 2014, 2016 and 2017, and advises that labels may show methylhexanamine, geranamine, 1,3-dimethylamylamine, geranium extract or Pelargonium graveolens extract.

Elsewhere, Health Canada ruled in July 2011 that it was a drug and banned sales; Sweden issued a warning in June 2012; Brazil's ANVISA added it to its prohibited list in 2012; Australia banned it in 2012, with New South Wales classing it as a highly dangerous substance; the UK's MHRA ruled in August 2012 that Jack3D was an unlicensed medicine; and New Zealand banned sales in 2012 [1].

FDA seized DMAA products from Hi-Tech Pharmaceuticals in 2013. A court ruled in April 2017 that they were adulterated, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed in 2019, the Supreme Court declined review in 2020 and the products were destroyed on 12 November 2020 [1].

WADA prohibits it. Wikipedia lists sanctions across sports, including an AFL player in 2011, minor league baseball players in 2012, a boxer in 2012, MotoGP rider Anthony West, whose ban was extended to 18 months in 2013, athletes at the 2014 Sochi Olympics, and a 2017 IOC decision to disqualify Jamaica's 2008 Olympic 4x100 relay team after a positive test by Nesta Carter [1]. T Nation threads about drug-tested 'natural' contests list it among prohibited stimulants [12].

Discussion peaked on bodybuilding forums around 2010 to 2012, when it was a headline ingredient in popular pre-workouts; members posted experiences ranging from enthusiasm to anxiety, and some asked whether it would be a problem for drug-tested events [2][8][9][3]. Posts also note its status as banned in Canada and its reputation among supplement-store staff [12]. More recent looksmax.org discussion treats it as a product sought out by name despite its restricted status [10].

A randomized trial gave 50 healthy young men placebo, caffeine, DMAA or both daily for 12 weeks to examine safety markers [5]. A pharmacokinetic study of eight men measured DMAA's physiological responses and blood levels [6]. A randomized trial examined the effects of DMAA and caffeine on heart rate and blood pressure in healthy men and women [7]. A 2012 paper analyzed whether DMAA in supplements matches natural or synthetic origin [4]. No trial examined appearance outcomes such as body composition or physique change.

lore.intro: On bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums DMAA is discussed mainly as a powerful pre-workout stimulant that was popular around 2010-2012 and later became hard to find or risky to use in tested sport [2][9][3][10].
